title: Contralateral Carotid Stenosis, Selective Shunting, and Early Stroke after Carotid Endarterectomy: A Retrospective Cohort Study
content: Background: Contralateral internal carotid artery stenosis may reduce collateral cerebral perfusion during carotid cross-clamping and influence endarterectomy management. We investigated early permanent stroke in the complete consecutive cohort and explored operative practices in patients with complete longer-term follow-up. Methods: This retrospective single-center study identified 123 carotid endarterectomy patients treated from January 2015 through December 2020. Seven-day stroke status was available for all patients: 43 with contralateral stenosis ≥50% and 80 with <50%. Detailed baseline, operative, and three-month outcomes were available in 98 patients (25 and 73, respectively). Intraoperative cerebral oxygenation was monitored using near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS); shunting was selective. Results: One imaging-confirmed permanent ischemic stroke occurred within seven postoperative days in each group (1/43 [2.3%] versus 1/80 [1.3%]; two-sided Fisher exact p = 1.000). Among the 98 patients with detailed data, selective shunting was used in 13/25 (52.0%) versus 0/73, and patch angioplasty in 18/25 (72.0%) versus 0/73 (both p < 0.001). Mean intensive care stay was 27.4 ± 18.1 versus 18.8 ± 2.4 hours. Conclusions: Early stroke was infrequent, but only two events preclude reliable risk comparisons or equivalence claims. The substantially different shunting and closure patterns in the 98-patient subset reflect clinical decision-making and are subject to confounding. Differential availability of longer-term data limits generalizability.
